about: Which ideas the site teaches and where. Each concept lists the lessons that teach it at each level (core, with a note on what that level adds), lessons that lean on it (uses), the films that show it and neighbouring ideas (near). Written offline by AI models from the lessons themselves (scripts/topic-graph), merged into one id per idea, read again by a second model that did not write it, and checked in CI by scripts/check-topic-graph.mjs. A lesson record is tied to the lesson's teaching text by hash; refresh with scripts/topic-graph/assign.mjs after a rewrite. Titles, courses and levels are not stored here: the site joins them at build time.

active-transport.name: Active transport and transport proteins
active-transport.blurb: Membrane proteins move ions and sugars across: channels and carriers let them run downhill, and pumps spend energy to push them uphill.
active-transport.subject: biology
aliases: how do cells move things uphill

rungs.adds: One ATP moves three sodium out and two potassium in, both uphill.
Channels and carriers pick the solute, never the direction; pumps pay with ATP.
Channels and carriers run downhill; pumping 3 mol of sodium out costs 39.6 kJ.

near.why: Every pump builds a gradient, and the gradient's two pushes decide which way an ion moves once a channel opens.
Nerve pulses run on ions rushing down gradients that sodium-potassium pumps built beforehand.
Pumping salt out of or into a cell changes where water goes, which is how animals keep their cells from swelling.

autophagy.name: Autophagy
autophagy.blurb: A cell wraps worn-out parts of itself in a membrane and digests them in the lysosome.
autophagy.subject: biology
aliases: how cells recycle their own parts

rungs.adds: Autophagosomes deliver cargo to lysosomes; LC3-II flux with bafilomycin separates making from clearing.

near.why: The proteasome is the cell's other way to clear unwanted material, used for single proteins instead of whole parts.
When a cell cannot clear its damage, it may be removed entirely, and autophagy helps decide which happens.
Neurons cannot dilute their waste by dividing, so clumped proteins and failing cleanup mark many brain diseases.

biomolecular-condensates.name: Condensates and phase separation
biomolecular-condensates.blurb: Some cell bodies with no membrane form when certain molecules gather into dense droplets that stay apart from the rest.
biomolecular-condensates.subject: biology

rungs.adds: Add more protein: droplets grow bigger, fixed sites only get brighter, until full.

near.why: Molecules that avoid water cluster together, and crowded, sticky proteins can pack into droplets in a similar way.
Droplets hold together through many weak contacts that break and re-form, so their contents can move in and out.
Some droplets harden into solid clumps, which is one proposed route to diseases where proteins aggregate in neurons.

cancer-drug-resistance.name: Drug resistance in cancer
cancer-drug-resistance.blurb: A tumour can change a drug's target so the drug no longer fits, and the change guides the next drug.
cancer-drug-resistance.subject: biology
aliases: why do cancer drugs stop working

rungs.adds: Imatinib fails when threonine 315 becomes isoleucine; the escape guides the next drug.

near.why: Survivors of a drug multiply and take over, whether the cells are bacteria in a patient or tumour cells.
Resistance starts as a chance DNA change in the drug's target, which then spreads because the drug removes the others.
A tumour treated with a drug is a population where cells that survive the drug leave more descendants.
Many cancer drugs block this receptor enzyme, and a change in its shape is a common way resistance appears.

cell-adhesion.name: Cell adhesion (cadherins and integrins)
cell-adhesion.blurb: Cells hold on to their neighbours and to the matrix around them through proteins linked to the cell's own filaments.
cell-adhesion.subject: biology

rungs.adds: Four links from partner to cable: predict where skin splits when one fails.
Talin switches the grip on from inside; clustered integrins build a signaling focal adhesion.

near.why: A crawling cell must grab the surface at its front and let go at its back, using the same adhesion proteins.
Adhesion proteins are what bind neighbouring cells into a sheet that lines the gut or covers the skin.
Tumour cells that lose their grip on neighbours can leave the tissue and spread to new places.
Developing neurons use sticky surface proteins to find the cells they should connect with.

cell-cycle-checkpoints.name: Cell cycle checkpoints
cell-cycle-checkpoints.blurb: A cell holds its next step until the last one is finished, so it does not divide with damaged or unsorted chromosomes.
cell-cycle-checkpoints.subject: biology
aliases: why cells stop dividing when their DNA is damaged

rungs.adds: Irradiated rad9 yeast repair when held in G2: the gene was for waiting.

near.why: A checkpoint stops the cycle when DNA is damaged, buying time for repair enzymes to fix it first.
Genes such as p53 hold the checkpoint brake, so losing them lets damaged cells keep dividing.
When the spindle checkpoint fails, daughter cells can receive too many or too few chromosomes.
A checkpoint works by holding back the kinase that drives the cycle.

cell-cycle-engine.name: The cell cycle engine (cyclins and CDKs)
cell-cycle-engine.blurb: A kinase switched on by a partner protein that builds up and is destroyed drives a cell through its cycle.
cell-cycle-engine.subject: biology

rungs.adds: A cyclin builds up and is destroyed at every division, switching CDK on.

near.why: The engine decides when a cell divides; this is how it splits.
Checkpoints hold the engine back until the last step is finished.
Destroying the cyclin is what makes each step one-way.

cell-death.name: Programmed cell death
cell-death.blurb: Cells can destroy themselves on purpose, and bodies use this to shape tissues and remove damaged cells.
cell-death.subject: biology
aliases: how does a body get rid of old cells

rungs.adds: A worm loses the same 131 cells every time: death as a program.
Fas gathers caspase-8 from outside; BAX and BAK free cytochrome c inside.
Why an embryo makes too many neurons, then lets the target choose.
Cytochrome c injected into NGF-fed neurons does not kill them: NGF holds two brakes.

near.why: Many young neurons die unless this signal reaches them.
A tissue keeps its size by balancing new cells against lost ones.
Immune cells both trigger this program and clear up after it.

cell-division.name: Cell division (mitosis)
cell-division.blurb: A cell copies its chromosomes, then splits so each new cell gets a full set.
cell-division.subject: biology
aliases: where do new cells come from

rungs.adds: Copy first, then share: heal a scrape one cell at a time.
The full cycle, G1 to M, with chromosomes and chromatids counted.
How the spindle grips each chromosome, checks the grip, then pulls.
Push the spindle aside and the RhoA band, then the furrow, follows.
Numb gathers in one daughter and vetoes Notch, so fly sisters differ.

near.why: The other way to divide: two rounds, half the chromosomes, for sex cells.
The copying step that has to finish before a cell divides.
One reason cells divide is that a big cell runs short of surface.
Bodies are shaped by cells dying on schedule as well as dividing.

cell-membrane.name: The cell membrane
cell-membrane.blurb: Every cell is wrapped in a double layer of fatty molecules with proteins, which lets some things cross and keeps others out.
cell-membrane.subject: biology
aliases: what is the cell membrane made of

rungs.adds: Two rows of phospholipids with proteins: what passes and what is kept out.
The two leaflets differ: flippases keep PS inside, and FRAP times sideways movement.
Head groups set charge and side: PS sits inside until apoptosis.
Bilayers self-assemble, and water crosses ten billion times faster than sodium.

near.why: The fatty acid tails that make up the bilayer decide whether the membrane is stiff or fluid.
Water pushes oily tails together, and that push is what assembles lipids into a double layer without any help.
Pores in the membrane let charged ions pass that the fatty layer would otherwise block, and nerve cells depend on them.
The bilayer exists because water pulls on itself and pushes away oily molecules, so lipids arrange themselves around it.

cell-migration.name: How cells crawl (cell migration)
cell-migration.blurb: A cell crawls by pushing its front out with actin, gripping the surface, pulling its body forward and letting go behind.
cell-migration.subject: biology

rungs.adds: Edge speed is polymerization minus retrograde flow: 40 minus 25 nm/s.

near.why: A growing nerve fibre moves by the same front-pushing crawl, steered by chemical cues it reads along the way.
Newborn neurons crawl long distances through the developing brain to reach the layer where they will work.
White blood cells crawl through tissue toward an infection, following chemical signals released by damaged cells.
Tumour cells that learn to crawl through surrounding tissue can enter blood vessels and spread to other organs.

cell-reprogramming.name: Turning cells back into stem cells (reprogramming)
cell-reprogramming.blurb: A specialized cell can be reset to a state that makes any cell type, by nuclear transfer or a few factors.
cell-reprogramming.subject: biology
aliases: turning a skin cell into a stem cell
can a specialized cell be reset

rungs.adds: Gurdon's tadpole nuclei to Yamanaka's four factors: how far a nucleus can reset.
Yamanaka screened 24 genes with an Fbx15 drug-resistance reporter, then narrowed to four.

near.why: Reprogramming produces cells that can make any type, which is the ability natural stem cells keep in the body.
Resetting a cell means erasing the marks that held its genes on or off, with no change to DNA letters.
Reset stem cells grown in a dish can organize into small pieces of tissue for studying disease.
A few gene-switching proteins are enough to reset a cell, because a cell's type depends on the mix it carries.

cell-size.name: Why cells are small
cell-size.blurb: As a cell grows, its inside outgrows its surface, so big living things are made of many small cells.
cell-size.subject: biology
aliases: could a cell be as big as a basketball
why are elephants made of tiny cells

rungs.adds: Build a cell from cubes and watch the surface fall behind the inside.
Dividing as the answer: test a surface-to-volume model of a growing cell.
Put rates on it: the radius where uptake can no longer meet demand.
Why a cell ten times wider needs membranes on the inside.

near.why: Small size matters because diffusion only works over short distances.
Inner membranes are how a big cell gets its surface back.
A cell that has grown too big for its surface can divide.

cell-size-control.name: How a cell senses its size
cell-size-control.blurb: Cells have no ruler, so they judge size from signals that change with growth, such as a brake that growth dilutes.
cell-size-control.subject: biology
aliases: how does a cell know how big it is
how cells decide to divide at the right size

rungs.adds: Dilute the brake Whi5 and budding yeast knows when to start dividing.

near.why: A cell grows only when growth factors and amino acids both signal that conditions are good.
A cell enters division only once it has reached a size that makes the split worthwhile.
Whole animals also change their rate of energy use with size, so bigger bodies are not just more small cells.

cell-theory.name: Cells, the unit of life
cell-theory.blurb: Every living thing is made of cells, and every cell comes from another cell.
cell-theory.subject: biology
aliases: what are living things made of
is everything alive made of cells

rungs.adds: Why cells stayed hidden until microscopes, and the three parts of the theory.
Six ideas, and the 175 years of evidence it took to earn them.

near.why: Once you know cells exist, the next question is what is inside one.
The theory's third part says cells come from cells; this is how.
Why living things are built from many small cells and not one big one.
Nerve tissue was the last place the theory was tested, and it took an electron microscope.

characteristics-of-life.name: What makes something alive (characteristics of life)
characteristics-of-life.blurb: Living things are made of cells, use energy, grow, respond and reproduce, and no single feature settles whether something is alive.
characteristics-of-life.subject: biology
aliases: how do you know if something is alive

rungs.adds: Build a checklist of life, then test a seed, a car, a leaf.
Run the checklist on a bacterium, virus, red blood cell and salt crystal.

near.why: A virus carries genes and evolves but cannot make its own energy or copy itself, so it fits only some items.
The first feature on the list, being made of cells, became a rule once microscopes showed cells in everything alive.
People once thought a special force separated living from nonliving matter, until experiments made life's molecules in a flask.

cilia.name: Cilia and flagella
cilia.blurb: Beating cilia and sperm tails bend as motor proteins slide their inner microtubules, which moves fluid or drives a cell along.
cilia.subject: biology

rungs.adds: Dynein sliding in a 9+2 axoneme becomes bending; Afzelius's four patients.

Dynein motors slide the microtubules inside a cilium past each other, and that sliding is what bends it.
A sperm reaches the egg only by beating its tail, a cilium-type structure, so a faulty one can cause infertility.

clonal-expansion.name: Mutant clones in healthy tissue
clonal-expansion.blurb: In healthy tissue a mutant cell's family can spread by keeping more daughters as dividing cells, until neighbours limit it.
clonal-expansion.subject: biology

A mutation that makes cells divide more often lets that clone outgrow its neighbours inside one body.

cytoskeleton.name: The cytoskeleton
cytoskeleton.blurb: A cell is shaped by a frame of three kinds of protein filament that it keeps taking apart and rebuilding.
cytoskeleton.subject: biology

A neuron's long axon and branched dendrites hold their shape and carry cargo along tracks made of filaments.
Microtubules build the spindle that pulls chromosomes apart, then an actin ring pinches the cell in two.

diffusion.name: Diffusion
diffusion.blurb: Particles spread from where they are crowded to where they are not, with no push needed.
diffusion.subject: biology
aliases: why does a smell spread across a room
how does oxygen get into cells
things spreading out on their own
moving from high to low concentration

Fast across a cell, hopeless across a body: time grows with distance squared.
Fick's law: why lungs and gills are large, thin and moist.

How far a signal reaches before it is cleared: distance, lifetime and dilution.

Diffusion is quick only over short distances, which keeps cells small.
A synapse is a gap narrow enough for diffusion to be fast.

dynamic-instability.name: Dynamic instability and treadmilling
dynamic-instability.blurb: Actin and tubulin filaments can grow at one end while shrinking at the other, or switch suddenly between growing and collapsing.
dynamic-instability.subject: biology

Tubulin switches between growing and collapsing according to whether it holds GTP or has cut it.

electrochemical-gradient.name: Electrochemical gradient (Nernst potential)
electrochemical-gradient.blurb: An ion moves according to two pushes at once: its concentration difference and the voltage across the membrane.
electrochemical-gradient.subject: biology

A nerve pulse is sodium and then potassium ions moving down their gradients as channels open in order.

endocytosis.name: Endocytosis
endocytosis.blurb: A cell takes things in by folding a patch of its surface membrane inward and pinching it off as a bubble.
endocytosis.subject: biology

Coated pit, dynamin cut, early endosome: where a taken-in receptor is sorted.

White blood cells engulf bacteria by wrapping membrane around them, then digest them inside the cell.

epithelium.name: Epithelia (sheets of cells)

epithelium.subject: biology

how the gut lining absorbs glucose

extracellular-matrix.name: The extracellular matrix
extracellular-matrix.blurb: Cells fill the space between them with a material they make, which carries pulling forces, resists squeezing and stores growth signals.
extracellular-matrix.subject: biology
aliases: what is the material between cells

ion-channels.name: Ion channels
ion-channels.blurb: An ion channel is a protein pore that opens to let certain ions flow across a membrane and change its voltage.
ion-channels.subject: biology
aliases: why potassium passes but sodium does not

lipid-asymmetry.name: Different lipids on each face of a membrane
lipid-asymmetry.blurb: The two halves of a membrane hold different lipids, and energy-using pumps keep it that way.
lipid-asymmetry.subject: biology
aliases: why phosphatidylserine faces the inside of the cell

Lipids on the inner face carry phosphates that proteins read to find where to go.

membrane-protein-topology.name: Which way a membrane protein faces (topology)

membrane-protein-topology.subject: biology
aliases: type I and type II membrane proteins
which way does a membrane protein face
why a sugar added in the ER ends up outside the cell

motor-proteins.name: Motor proteins

motor-proteins.subject: biology
aliases: how cargo moves inside a cell

Bubbles of cargo ride motors along tracks to reach the compartment where they should deliver.

nuclear-organization.name: How the nucleus is organized

nuclear-organization.subject: biology

nuclear-transport.name: Nuclear import and export

nuclear-transport.subject: biology

organelle-inheritance.name: How organelles are shared at division

organelle-inheritance.subject: biology
aliases: how organelles are shared when a cell divides
how mitochondria are split between daughter cells

organelles.name: Organelles: the parts of a cell
organelles.blurb: A cell has small parts inside it, each with a job, and they work together.
organelles.subject: biology
aliases: difference between plant and animal cells

rungs.adds: Switch off one part of a model cell and see what stops.
The three parts plant cells add: wall, chloroplasts and a big water tank.
Follow insulin from gene to export, one organelle handing to the next.

Matrix near pH 8 down to acid lysosomes, each compartment's pH set by pumps.

Mitochondria are where most of a cell's energy is released.
Chloroplasts are the organelle where plants catch light.
The nucleus holds the gene; ribosomes build what it codes for.

osmosis.name: Osmosis
osmosis.blurb: Water moves across a membrane toward the side with more dissolved stuff.
osmosis.subject: biology
aliases: why does salt make cucumbers wet
why do cells swell in water
why does limp lettuce get crisp in water

In distilled water a red blood cell may burst; a plant cell's wall holds.
Count dissolved particles, then ask how a sea fish keeps its water.
Water potential: one number that says which way water will cross.
Where a litre of water goes in your body, and why saline differs.

Osmosis fills a plant's cells; a different pull lifts water up the stem.
Your body holds its water and salt steady with feedback loops.

primary-cilium.name: The primary cilium
primary-cilium.blurb: Many cells carry one hairlike projection that does not beat and works as an antenna for signals.
primary-cilium.subject: biology
aliases: what does the primary cilium do

rungs.adds: Smoothened enters the cilium: mutants that cannot build one cannot answer Hedgehog.

protein-degradation.name: Protein degradation (ubiquitin and the proteasome)

protein-degradation.subject: biology

protein-quality-control.name: Protein quality control and ER stress

protein-quality-control.subject: biology

protein-sorting.name: Protein sorting (signal sequences)

protein-sorting.subject: biology

rho-gtpases.name: Rho, Rac and Cdc42

rho-gtpases.subject: biology

A repulsive cue makes the growth cone fold up by acting on the switches that control its actin.
Rac builds a crawling cell's front and Rho pulls its back, so the two switches decide which way it moves.

secretory-pathway.name: The secretory pathway
secretory-pathway.blurb: A protein made for export travels from the rough ER through the Golgi to the cell surface, changed along the way.
secretory-pathway.subject: biology
aliases: path of a secreted protein through the cell
ER to Golgi to cell surface

Sugar chains are added to proteins in the Golgi as they travel, which is how surface labels are made.

stem-cell-niche.name: The stem cell niche

stem-cell-niche.subject: biology
aliases: what keeps a stem cell a stem cell
Wnt and BMP in the gut crypt

stem-cells.name: Stem cells

stem-cells.subject: biology

sugar-coat.name: The sugar coat and lectins

vesicle-transport.subject: biology
aliases: how do vesicles find where to go

allostery.name: Allostery and cooperativity
allostery.blurb: A protein flips between a weak-grip and a tight-grip shape, so binding at one site changes the others.
allostery.subject: biology

why is the hemoglobin oxygen curve s shaped

amino-acids.name: Amino acids and their side chains
amino-acids.blurb: Twenty amino acids share one backbone and differ in their side chain, which sets charge and how well it mixes with water.
amino-acids.subject: biology

antimetabolite-drugs.name: Antimetabolite drugs

antimetabolite-drugs.subject: biology

A drug that resembles an enzyme's normal molecule can sit in its active site and block it.

carbohydrates.name: Carbohydrates (sugars and starch)

carbohydrates.subject: biology

near.why: Sugar chains on cell surfaces work as labels that other proteins read.
Plants build sugar and starch from carbon dioxide and water using light.

Gut enzymes cut starch into sugars small enough to absorb.

cholesterol.name: Cholesterol: making it and taking it up
cholesterol.blurb: Cells build cholesterol from acetyl-CoA or import it from LDL, and one sensor in the ER membrane controls both.
cholesterol.subject: biology

enzymes.name: Enzymes
enzymes.blurb: Enzymes are proteins that make the reactions of life go fast enough to keep you alive.
enzymes.subject: biology
aliases: why does fresh pineapple stop gelatin setting
how does the body speed up reactions

An enzyme is a protein, and a gene holds the order of its parts.

hydrophobic-effect.name: The hydrophobic effect
hydrophobic-effect.blurb: Water pushes oily groups together because that frees the water, which helps fold proteins and build membranes.
hydrophobic-effect.subject: biology
aliases: why oil and water do not mix
why nonpolar molecules clump in water

Water holds on to itself with hydrogen bonds, so oily things cannot mix in.

lipids.name: Lipids and fatty acids
lipids.blurb: Fats and oils are built from fatty acid tails; straight tails pack and stay solid, bent ones stay liquid.
lipids.subject: biology
aliases: why is butter solid and oil liquid

rungs.adds: One cis bend turns solid lard into liquid olive oil: oleate versus palmitate.

Cholesterol is a fat-like molecule that cells build or import, and it changes how a membrane behaves.

macromolecules.name: The molecules of life (macromolecules)
macromolecules.blurb: Living things are built from four kinds of large molecule: carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids and lipids, each made of smaller building blocks.
macromolecules.subject: biology
aliases: why is life based on carbon

rungs.adds: Four classes, their blocks and jobs: starch and cellulose differ by one link.

near.why: DNA is the nucleic acid that stores a living thing's instructions.

Digestion cuts the large molecules in food into small building blocks the body can absorb.
Cells build proteins by reading genes, which shows how one kind of large molecule makes another.

nucleotide-metabolism.name: Making and recycling nucleotides
nucleotide-metabolism.blurb: Cells build nucleotides at high cost, so they recycle free bases and break down the rest.
nucleotide-metabolism.subject: biology
aliases: where does uric acid come from

rungs.adds: Build a purine for about 6 ATP, recycle a free base for 2.

near.why: Drugs that look like nucleotide building blocks jam these pathways and stop fast-dividing cells copying DNA.
Purines that are not recycled end up as uric acid, which can form crystals in joints.
The five-carbon sugar in every nucleotide comes from this side path off glucose.

ph-and-buffers.name: pH and buffers
ph-and-buffers.blurb: pH tells how acidic a solution is; it decides which groups carry charge, and buffers keep it steady.
ph-and-buffers.subject: biology

rungs.adds: Predict charge from pH minus pKa; bicarbonate holds blood at 7.35 to 7.45.

Amino acid side chains pick up or lose charge with pH, which changes how a protein acts.
Stomach lining cells pump out acid strong enough to drop the stomach's pH very low.

properties-of-water.name: Water's special properties (polarity and hydrogen bonds)
properties-of-water.blurb: Water molecules have charged ends that tug on each other, so water dissolves salt, sticks together and clings to surfaces.
properties-of-water.subject: biology
aliases: why does salt dissolve in water

rungs.adds: Bent, polar molecule: hydrogen bonds explain salt, strider and towel.

protein-binding.name: Binding strength (affinity and Kd)

protein-binding.subject: biology
aliases: how tightly does a protein hold its ligand

A hormone in a sample is measured by how it competes with a labelled copy for scarce antibody.

protein-folding.name: Protein folding
protein-folding.blurb: A chain of amino acids finds its working shape by itself, and fast, because its sequence holds the instructions.
protein-folding.subject: biology

Water pushing oily groups together is a main force that drives a chain to fold.
In some diseases of adult life, misfolded proteins clump in the tissue while particular nerve cells die.

protein-structure.name: Protein structure
protein-structure.blurb: A protein chain coils into helices and sheets and packs into a 3D shape, and that shape decides its job.
protein-structure.subject: biology
aliases: primary secondary tertiary and quaternary structure

rungs.adds: Two hinges per residue, the Ramachandran map, helices, sheets and a buried core.

near.why: The shape of a pocket in an enzyme decides which molecule it can change.
Small folds recognize a short sequence or lipid, so shape decides who a protein partners with.
Hemoglobin changes shape when it picks up oxygen, and that shift is how blood loads and unloads it.

specific-heat.name: Specific heat (why water warms slowly)
specific-heat.blurb: Some materials need more energy than others to warm up; water needs a lot, so it warms and cools slowly.
specific-heat.subject: biology
aliases: why sand gets hotter than water

rungs.adds: Water versus sand, then a Bay buoy: air swung 8 °C, water 1.4.

near.why: Bodies are mostly water, so they warm and cool slowly, which helps animals hold a steady temperature.

Hydrogen bonds between water molecules are the reason water needs so much energy to warm.

vitalism.name: Vitalism and its fall
vitalism.blurb: People once thought only living things could make the molecules of life; experiments showed chemistry can.
vitalism.subject: biology
aliases: can chemistry make the molecules of life

rungs.adds: Wöhler's urea in 1828 to Buchner's cell-free fermentation in 1897.

weak-interactions.name: Weak bonds (noncovalent interactions)
weak-interactions.blurb: Hydrogen bonds, ionic attractions and van der Waals contacts are weak enough to break and re-form, and cells run on them.
weak-interactions.subject: biology

rungs.adds: Bonds worth one or two RT: why water evens out ionic and hydrogen bonds.

Hydrogen bonds between base pairs hold the two DNA strands together yet let them come apart for copying.
Many small weak contacts, added up, hold a folded chain in its working shape.

amino-acid-catabolism.name: Using amino acids as fuel (amino acid catabolism)
amino-acid-catabolism.blurb: After the nitrogen is removed, the carbon of each amino acid is burned for energy or turned into glucose or ketones.
amino-acid-catabolism.subject: biology
aliases: how the body burns protein for energy

rungs.adds: Seven entry doors for carbon; only Leu and Lys are purely ketogenic.

Carbon from amino acids is one of the raw materials the liver turns into new glucose.
Some amino acid carbon ends up as ketones, fuel for the brain in a long fast.
Muscle protein is burned for fuel as fasting goes on, which shows when this pathway matters most.

ampk-energy-sensing.name: How cells sense low energy (AMPK)
ampk-energy-sensing.blurb: When a cell runs low on energy, AMP rises, and the enzyme AMPK switches off costly jobs and turns on fuel use.
ampk-energy-sensing.subject: biology

Muscle AMPK turns on during exercise and pulls sugar from the blood without needing insulin.

atp.name: ATP, the cell's energy carrier
atp.blurb: ATP is a small molecule that cells spend to power their work, then rebuild from ADP and phosphate.
atp.subject: biology

Pumps in the cell membrane spend ATP to push ions where they would not go alone.
Motor proteins burn ATP to walk along tracks inside the cell and carry cargo.

cellular-respiration.name: Cellular respiration

cellular-respiration.subject: biology

how cells break down sugar with oxygen

All ten steps of splitting glucose, and why the cell spends ATP first.
One machine, three enzymes, five coenzymes: pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, CO₂ and NADH.

chemiosmosis.name: Chemiosmosis (the proton gradient that makes ATP)

Pumps spend energy to push ions uphill, and here ions rolling back downhill make ATP.

citric-acid-cycle.name: The citric acid cycle (Krebs cycle)

fatty-acid-oxidation.name: Burning fat (beta-oxidation)

fatty-acid-synthesis.name: Making fat (fatty acid synthesis)

gluconeogenesis.name: Making new glucose (gluconeogenesis)

new glucose from lactate and amino acids

glycolysis.name: Glycolysis

glycolysis.subject: biology

ketone-bodies.name: Ketone bodies

metabolic-rate.name: Metabolic rate

metabolic-scaling.subject: biology

pentose-phosphate-pathway.name: The pentose phosphate pathway

pentose-phosphate-pathway.subject: biology

photosynthesis.name: Photosynthesis

photosynthesis.subject: biology
aliases: where does the wood in a tree come from

urea-cycle.name: The urea cycle

urea-cycle.subject: biology

Birds and humans end purine breakdown at uric acid, another way to dispose of nitrogen.

aneuploidy.name: Extra or missing chromosomes (aneuploidy)

aneuploidy.subject: biology

bacterial-gene-transfer.name: How bacteria swap genes

bacterial-gene-transfer.subject: biology

biochemical-pathway-mutants.name: Mutants that reveal a metabolic pathway

cancer.name: Cancer as a genetic disease

chromosome-rearrangements.name: Chromosome rearrangements

complementation-test.subject: biology

genome-size.name: Genome size (how much DNA)

immediate-early-genes.name: Immediate early genes

rungs.adds: Breed once or repeatedly? A finite budget, guppy transplants and brood-enlargement tests.

mass-extinction.name: Mass extinctions
mass-extinction.blurb: Now and then most species on Earth die out within a short stretch of geological time.
mass-extinction.subject: biology

rungs.adds: Over three-quarters of species lost: the Big Five, and iridium at the end-Cretaceous.

molecular-clock.name: The molecular clock

molecular-clock.subject: biology

calibrating a molecular clock with fossils

near.why: The clock ticks because new mutations build up in a gene at a fairly steady average rate.
The clock needs the sequences of the same gene from two species, read letter by letter.
A gene under strong selection changes at a different rate, so the clock must be checked for it.

natural-selection.name: Natural selection
natural-selection.blurb: Living things that fit their surroundings leave more offspring, so helpful inherited traits become more common.
natural-selection.subject: biology
aliases: why did the moths turn dark
how do species change over time
do animals change on purpose to survive

rungs.adds: Be the hungry bird: which yarn worms get eaten last?

Poaching in Gorongosa raised tuskless females from 18.5 to 50.9 percent.

Relative fitness of moth morphs, stabilizing galls, disruptive sticklebacks and the widowbird tail.

near.why: An adaptation is what selection leaves behind.
Where the differences that selection sorts come from.
Selection is the how; fossils and DNA are the record that it happened.
A trait can spread only if offspring inherit it.

neanderthal-ancestry.name: Neanderthal and Denisovan DNA in living people
neanderthal-ancestry.blurb: Some of our ancestors had children with Neanderthals and Denisovans, so many living people carry a little of their DNA.
neanderthal-ancestry.subject: biology

When two human groups meet and have children, gene versions flow from one population into the other.

origin-of-modern-humans.name: Where modern humans came from
origin-of-modern-humans.blurb: Our species arose in Africa from connected populations, not at one birthplace on one date.
origin-of-modern-humans.subject: biology

rungs.adds: Jebel Irhoud, Omo I and Misliya: ask what each fossil date measured.

near.why: Connected populations across Africa exchanged mates, so no single place and time holds the whole origin.
Modern humans met other human groups outside Africa and had children with them.
Comparing DNA of people from different regions shows that African populations hold the most variety.

phylogenetic-trees.name: Evolutionary trees (phylogenetic trees)
phylogenetic-trees.blurb: A branching diagram shows how living things are related; the closest relatives share the most recent common ancestor.
phylogenetic-trees.subject: biology
aliases: how to read a phylogenetic tree

rungs.adds: Score five traits in six animals; the 1s nest into branches.
Trout is closer kin to you than to a shark: read the nodes.

near.why: Nested groups in a classification are meant to match the branches of the tree.
A tree with branch lengths from gene differences can be given dates.
Mapping a trait onto the tree shows whether it came from one ancestor or arose twice.

proximate-and-ultimate-causes.name: How questions and why questions in biology
proximate-and-ultimate-causes.blurb: A trait has a how answer, the body mechanism that builds it, and a why answer, the evolutionary history behind it.
proximate-and-ultimate-causes.subject: biology

rungs.adds: Stomatal density asked two ways; Mayr 1961 and Reznick's guppy fish.

near.why: A bird leaves in autumn because day length cues it, and the why is that winter food runs short.
The why answers in biology are told by selection acting on past generations.
A trait such as a thick coat has a body mechanism that builds it and a history that explains why it helps.

regulatory-evolution.name: Evolution of gene switches (enhancers)
regulatory-evolution.blurb: A body part can change when a gene's on-off switch changes, while the protein the gene makes stays the same.
regulatory-evolution.subject: biology
aliases: how can the body change without the protein changing

near.why: The switches that change are short DNA stretches where these proteins bind and set how often a gene is copied.

Cells with the same DNA already differ by which genes are on, so a change in the switch changes the animal.

selection-in-genes.name: Finding selection in gene sequences (dN/dS)
selection-in-genes.blurb: Comparing DNA changes that alter a protein with changes that do not shows where selection has acted on a gene.
selection-in-genes.subject: biology
aliases: how to detect positive selection in a gene

near.why: Some mutations change an amino acid and others do not, and counting each kind is what the test relies on.
The genetic code decides whether a letter change alters the protein or leaves it as it was.
Genes with few protein-changing differences keep a steadier rate, so they make better clocks.

speciation.name: Speciation (how new species form)
speciation.blurb: One species splits into two when separated groups build up barriers and stop interbreeding and producing fertile offspring.
speciation.subject: biology
aliases: what makes two groups separate species

rungs.adds: Split one finch population with a river; when do two halves count as species?

Speciation needs gene flow between the groups to be small enough that differences build up.
One ancestor splitting repeatedly into many species gives a radiation, as with finches on islands.

variation.name: Variation within a population
variation.blurb: Members of one kind of living thing differ in many traits, because of their genes, their surroundings and chance.
variation.subject: biology
aliases: why no two living things are exactly alike

rungs.adds: Peas from one pod, lined up by a ruler, are not the same.
Ten oak leaves from one tree and 12-year-old heights: two sources plus chance.
Chestnuts with little blight resistance: variation helps only if the trait is already there.
Mutation makes new alleles, gene flow moves them, sexual reproduction reshuffles them.

near.why: New gene versions start as changes in DNA, which is where a population's differences come from.
Eggs and sperm are made with shuffled chromosomes, so children differ from their parents and from each other.
Differences between two plants of one kind can come from their genes or from the soil and light they got.
Without differences between individuals, survival and breeding could not favour any trait over another.

animal-body-plans.name: Animal body plans
animal-body-plans.blurb: Animals are described by their symmetry, tissue layers, body cavity and gut, which show how each body is built.
animal-body-plans.subject: biology

rungs.adds: Symmetry, germ layers and cavities, then ten phyla in one line each.

near.why: A worm with no bones still moves, because fluid held inside its muscular body works as a skeleton.
Animals with a similar body build are not always close relatives, so build alone cannot show who descends from whom.
One insect can have two very different bodies in a lifetime, such as a caterpillar and then a moth.
Genes in a fixed order label body regions from head to tail, which sets how an animal's body is laid out.

biodiversity.name: Biodiversity (species diversity)
biodiversity.blurb: Biodiversity is the variety of living things in a place: how many kinds there are and how evenly they are shared.
biodiversity.subject: biology

rungs.adds: Dead zones, hurricanes and fires change which species stay, and recovery depends on severity.
Two plots, same four species: 25 each versus 40, 40, 10, 10.

near.why: Fields with more kinds of plants usually grow more and change less from year to year.
Storms, waves and fires reset a place, and how often they strike changes how many species live there.
An island's count of species settles where new arrivals balance losses, so size and distance matter.
Every species that dies out removes one kind from the count of what lives in a place.

classification.name: Classifying living things (taxonomy)
classification.blurb: Scientists sort living things into nested groups, from three domains down to species, by shared traits and how they are related.
classification.subject: biology
aliases: domain kingdom phylum class order family genus species

Ether-linked isoprenoid lipids back the rRNA split; many-gene trees nest eukaryotes near Asgard archaea.

near.why: A key puts the sorting into use: two-choice questions about visible traits lead you to a name.
Each species ends up with a two-part name that scientists in every country use the same way.
Matching genes between living things moved fungi beside animals and changed how the groups are drawn.
A branching tree of relatives shows why a proper group holds an ancestor and all of its descendants.

dichotomous-key.name: Dichotomous keys
dichotomous-key.blurb: A key names a living thing through a series of two-choice questions about traits you can see.
dichotomous-key.subject: biology
aliases: how to use a dichotomous key
identify a plant or animal with a key
how to identify a tree by its leaves

rungs.adds: Fins, jointed legs, hinged shell: a key finds a name, not relatives.

near.why: A key ends by naming the species, and the two-part name is what you then look up.
Keys are how you name the small creek animals whose kinds show whether a stream is clean.
The traits a key asks about work because living things sort into nested groups of relatives.

fungi.name: Fungi
fungi.blurb: Fungi digest food outside their bodies and absorb it, growing as threads or single yeast cells.
fungi.subject: biology

rungs.adds: Plasmogamy, dikaryon, karyogamy: fusion in two steps, plus root partners.

near.why: Fungi are a main reason dead leaves and logs rot and give their nutrients back to the soil.
Many fungi live around plant roots and trade minerals for sugar, and both partners gain.
Yeast, a single-celled fungus, makes the carbon dioxide that raises bread and the ethanol in beer.
Both absorb food from outside and rot dead matter, yet fungi have a nucleus and bacteria do not.

scientific-names.name: Scientific names (binomial nomenclature)
scientific-names.blurb: Each species has a two-part name, genus first, that scientists use the same way in every country.
scientific-names.subject: biology
aliases: why do scientists use latin names
how to write a scientific name

rungs.adds: Cathartes aura: why vulture and buzzard names clash, and one name fixes it.

A key walks you through two-choice questions until you can put a name on the plant or animal.
A name stands for one species, so it is only as sound as the decision about what counts as one.
Gene matches can show that two look-alikes are not close relatives, which can change what they are called.

species-concepts.name: What counts as a species
species-concepts.blurb: A species is a lineage evolving on its own, and biologists use several kinds of evidence to recognize one.
species-concepts.subject: biology
aliases: how do biologists tell two species apart

rungs.adds: Biological, ecological, phylogenetic and morphological criteria read as evidence of a separate lineage.

near.why: Where one species splits in two, the line is hard to draw, and that is the problem a species idea must solve.
Groups that keep trading genes stay one lineage, while groups that stop can drift into two.
Bacteria pass genes between distant kinds, which is one reason the species idea fits them badly.
Gene differences between two populations can show whether they are separate lineages.

biodiversity-ecosystem-function.name: Biodiversity and ecosystem function
biodiversity-ecosystem-function.blurb: Fields with more kinds of plants usually grow more and change less from year to year.
biodiversity-ecosystem-function.subject: biology

rungs.adds: Cedar Creek: 168 plots, 1 to 16 species, richer plots grew more.

near.why: Before asking what variety does for a field, learn how variety is counted: how many kinds, and how evenly shared.
The extra growth in mixed fields is a measured rate of plant energy capture, so this shows what is counted.
Plants with different needs share light, water and soil without crowding each other, which is why mixed fields do more.
Storms and fires change how many species a place holds, and so change the work those species do together.

carbon-cycle.name: The carbon cycle

climate.name: Climate and biomes
climate.blurb: Climate is a place's usual warmth and rain, set by sunlight and moving air, and it shapes what can live there.
climate.subject: biology

Warmth and rain set how much plants grow in a biome, and that sets how much food is there.
A lasting shift in warmth and rain changes which biomes a place can support.

climate-change.name: Climate change
climate-change.blurb: Climate change is a lasting shift in a place's usual temperature, rain or weather over many years.
climate-change.subject: biology

competition.name: Competition between species
competition.blurb: Living things that need the same scarce resource hold each other back, and sometimes one kind drives the other out.

why does the faster growing species not always win

Many invaders spread by taking food and space from native species.

conservation.name: Conservation and restoration
conservation.blurb: People protect living things and their habitats, remove what harms them, and help damaged places recover, often slowly and partly.
conservation.subject: biology

decomposers.name: Decomposers and decay

demography.name: Demography and life tables

demography.subject: biology

disturbance-and-diversity.name: Disturbance and diversity
disturbance-and-diversity.blurb: Storms, waves and fires reset communities, and how often and how hard they strike changes how many species live there.
disturbance-and-diversity.subject: biology

ecological-succession.name: Ecological succession
ecological-succession.blurb: After a disturbance or on new ground, the species in a place replace one another over time in a general order.
ecological-succession.subject: biology
aliases: what happens to an abandoned field over time
how a forest grows back after a fire
how does life return to bare rock

ecosystem.name: Ecosystems: living and nonliving parts
ecosystem.blurb: An ecosystem is the living things in a place together with the nonliving things around them, such as water, soil and sunlight.
ecosystem.subject: biology

erosion.name: Erosion (soil washing away)
erosion.blurb: Rain and wind carry soil away from bare ground, and plant roots and leaves slow it down.

why does a stream run muddy after a storm

extinction-risk-small-populations.name: Why small populations go extinct
extinction-risk-small-populations.blurb: Chance events can wipe out a small population, so safety is a chance of lasting a set time, not a fixed number.
extinction-risk-small-populations.subject: biology

food-webs.name: Food webs and energy flow

food-webs.subject: biology
aliases: why are there so few top predators
why does a hawk need grass

habitat.name: Habitats
habitat.blurb: A habitat is the place that gives a living thing the food, water, shelter and space it needs.
habitat.subject: biology

human-impact-on-ecosystems.name: How people change ecosystems

human-impact-on-ecosystems.subject: biology

invasive-species.name: Invasive species
invasive-species.blurb: An invasive species is brought to a new place, spreads, and harms native species or people.
invasive-species.subject: biology

island-biogeography.name: Island biogeography

island-biogeography.subject: biology
aliases: why do bigger islands have more species

keystone-species.name: Keystone species

keystone-species.subject: biology

Taking one species out of a food web changes everything linked to it, not only its prey.

limiting-factors.name: Limiting factors
limiting-factors.blurb: Food, water, space, disease, predators and weather can keep a population from growing larger.
limiting-factors.subject: biology

near.why: Each limiting factor works by raising deaths or lowering births, which is what slows a growing population.

metapopulation.name: Metapopulations
metapopulation.blurb: A species can last across many patches even when each patch's population dies out, if empty patches are settled again fast enough.
metapopulation.subject: biology

colonization and extinction of habitat patches

niche.name: The ecological niche

niche.subject: biology

what sets the edge of a species' range

nitrogen-cycle.name: The nitrogen cycle

nitrogen-cycle.subject: biology

where does the nitrogen in soil come from

Fungi and bacteria that rot dead plants and animals return their nitrogen to the soil.

nutrient-pollution.name: Watersheds and dead zones

nutrient-pollution.subject: biology

population-growth.name: Population growth and carrying capacity

near.why: Food, space, disease and predators are the specific things that slow growth as crowding rises.
Counting births and deaths at each age shows whether a population replaces itself.
Predator numbers rise and fall with prey numbers, which makes a population cycle instead of growing smoothly.

predation.name: Predators and prey
predation.blurb: Predators eat prey, so each population's numbers depend on the other's, and predators usually run short of food before prey run out.
predation.subject: biology
aliases: why predators do not eat all their prey
why do predator numbers peak after prey
wolves and moose on Isle Royale

rungs.adds: Moose per wolf as a clue, checked against Isle Royale counts, 1980 to 2026.
Lotka-Volterra ledgers: equilibrium N* = m/(ea), P* = r/a, and lagging peaks.

near.why: Removing one predator from a shore or forest can change many species, not only its prey.
Prey evolve defences and predators evolve ways around them, each changing the other over generations.
Each predator and prey pair is one link in a web that carries energy from plants upward.

primary-production.name: Primary production (GPP and NPP)
primary-production.blurb: Plants capture energy at a rate, and what they keep after their own respiration is the food for everything else.
primary-production.subject: biology
aliases: how do you measure photosynthesis in a whole ecosystem

rungs.adds: GPP, NPP and NEP as rates; light and dark bottles, harvests, flux towers.

near.why: Primary production is photosynthesis measured as a rate across a whole field or forest.
What the plant keeps is what remains after its own cells burn some sugar for energy.
The food left over after plant respiration is all the energy that animals can eat.
Plants pull carbon dioxide out of the air to make that food, and return some through respiration.

seasonal-responses.name: How living things meet the seasons
seasonal-responses.blurb: Animals and plants use cues like day length and temperature to migrate, hibernate or go dormant through hard seasons.
seasonal-responses.subject: biology
aliases: where do animals go in winter
why do trees drop their leaves in fall

rungs.adds: Sort ten Virginia animals into travel, rest or stay, then watch the window.
Migration, dormancy and hibernation: how monarchs, tree buds and groundhogs get through winter.

near.why: Some animals lower their body temperature on purpose through winter to save energy.
Plants measure the length of the night to tell the season and to time flowering.
The cues of day and night that set a daily body clock also feed the yearly one.

seasonal-rhythms.name: Seasonal rhythms (phenology)
seasonal-rhythms.blurb: Living things change through the year, cued by day length and temperature, and warming can shift when those changes happen.
seasonal-rhythms.subject: biology
aliases: why do trees lose their leaves in fall
how do animals get through winter
why are cherry blossoms blooming earlier

rungs.adds: Visit one tree monthly for a year: bare in winter, buds already waiting.
Washington cherry peak-bloom days since 1921 moved earlier after the 1960s, unsteadily.
Nine Dutch flycatcher populations fell 90% where caterpillars peaked early.

near.why: Plants measure night length with a pigment, which is how many of them know it is time to flower.
Warmer springs move leaf-out and nesting earlier, so timing shifts can be measured year by year.
When timing no longer fits a place, some species move to places where it still does.
Migration, dormancy and hibernation are what the yearly timing is for.

soil.name: What soil is made of
soil.blurb: Soil is a mix of sand, silt and clay, bits of dead plants, air and water.
soil.subject: biology

rungs.adds: Shake soil in water: sand sinks in a minute, clay takes a day.

near.why: Rain and wind can carry away soil from bare ground, which loses the dead plant bits it holds.
Fungi, bacteria and worms turn dead leaves into the dark crumbly part of soil.
Plants take minerals such as nitrogen and potassium from soil, and a shortage shows in their leaves.

species-range-shifts.name: Species on the move (range shifts)
species-range-shifts.blurb: As the climate warms, many living things shift where they live, toward the poles and up mountains.
species-range-shifts.subject: biology
aliases: species moving uphill as climate warms
why animals are moving toward the poles

rungs.adds: Isotherm speed is warming over gradient: 50 m uphill a decade, species 11 m.

near.why: Range shifts are the clearest sign that warming is already changing where living things can live.
A species moves because the warmth and rain its niche needs have moved to a new place.
Species that move or stay may find their yearly timing no longer matches food and weather.

stream-health-indicators.name: Creek animals as clues to water health
stream-health-indicators.blurb: The kinds of small animals living in a creek are a clue to how healthy the water is for wildlife.
stream-health-indicators.subject: biology
aliases: how to tell if a stream is healthy

rungs.adds: Count what lives under rocks: mayfly and stonefly young need clean, oxygen-rich water.

near.why: Fertilizer and sewage use up oxygen in creeks, which removes the animals that need clean water.
Soil washed into a creek buries the stones where its small animals live.
The number and kinds of creek animals together give a simple measure of variety.

symbiosis.name: Symbiosis: mutualism, commensalism and parasitism
symbiosis.blurb: In symbiosis, two different species live closely together, and each partner gains, loses or is unaffected.
symbiosis.subject: biology
aliases: why plant roots partner with fungi
is it a mutualist or a parasite

rungs.adds: Mutualism, commensalism, parasitism: sort by gain or loss, then test marigolds with root fungus.
Root fungus helps in poor soil, costs in rich; soybeans punish non-fixing rhizobia.

near.why: Whether partners help or harm each other can change as each evolves in response to the other.
Mitochondria began as bacteria living inside larger cells, a partnership that became permanent.
Microbes in the gut digest plant fiber the animal cannot, and the animal absorbs what they make.
Legumes feed bacteria in root nodules, and the bacteria give back nitrogen the plant can use.

water-cycle.name: The water cycle
water-cycle.blurb: Water evaporates, forms clouds, falls as rain or snow, then soaks in or runs off and returns to the sea and air.
water-cycle.subject: biology
aliases: where does rainwater go after it falls
what happens to water after it rains
how water moves between land, sky and sea

rungs.adds: Six steps from evaporation to runoff, and the leaf door shared with carbon.
Runoff and groundwater carry nitrogen, soil and germs from a field to the Bay.

near.why: Carbon dioxide enters a leaf through the same openings that water vapor leaves by.
Most water a plant takes up leaves through its leaves, so plants are part of the cycle.
Where water falls and how much of it falls set the warmth and rain of a biome.

alternation-of-generations.name: Alternation of generations
alternation-of-generations.blurb: A land plant lives as two bodies in turn: a haploid one that makes gametes and a diploid one that makes spores.
alternation-of-generations.subject: biology
aliases: what is the green part of moss

rungs.adds: Label every stage n or 2n: moss, fern, pine, and endosperm at 3n.

near.why: Meiosis is the step that ends the diploid body and makes the spores that start the haploid one.
Plants mix sexual and asexual reproduction in one life cycle, and so do many animals and fungi.
Over time the haploid body shrank and the diploid body grew, which helped plants cope with dry land.

double-fertilization.name: Double fertilization
double-fertilization.blurb: A pollen tube delivers two sperm: one starts the embryo and the other starts the seed's food store.
double-fertilization.subject: biology
aliases: how does pollen fertilize a flower

rungs.adds: Count chromosome sets in a maize kernel: yellow pollen, yellow ear.

near.why: Animal fertilization joins one sperm to one egg; flowering plants use two sperm for two different jobs.
The pollen grain that lands on the flower grows the tube that carries these two sperm down.
The embryo made here holds the first stem cells that later make every part of the plant.

leaf-pigments.name: Leaf colors (pigments)
leaf-pigments.blurb: Green leaves hold yellow and orange colors all summer, hidden by green chlorophyll that fades in fall.
leaf-pigments.subject: biology
aliases: why do leaves change color in fall
where does the yellow in a fall leaf come from

rungs.adds: Pull the green out of a leaf and find the yellow hiding under it.

near.why: Chlorophyll is the pigment that catches light for photosynthesis, and the yellow and orange pigments help it.
Fall color is one of the easiest seasonal changes to watch and record year after year.
Our eyes tell leaf colors apart using three kinds of cone cells that respond to different light.

meristems.name: How plants grow longer (meristems)
meristems.blurb: Plants grow from patches of cells that keep dividing, mostly at the tips of roots and shoots.
meristems.subject: biology
aliases: where do plants add new cells

rungs.adds: One cell an hour, then lengthening from 15 to 300 micrometers: root growth.

near.why: A meristem is a plant's stem cell zone: some cells keep dividing while their daughters become tissue.
Growth at a root tip is cells dividing and then stretching, so you can see mitosis in an onion root.
Meristem cells stay undivided because of signals from neighbouring cells, as animal stem cells do in their niche.

nitrogen-fixation.name: Nitrogen fixation and root nodules
nitrogen-fixation.blurb: Some bacteria turn nitrogen gas from the air into ammonia, and legumes house them in root nodules.
nitrogen-fixation.subject: biology

rungs.adds: Hellriegel and Wilfarth's peas: live soil extract gave nodules and nitrogen gain; heated, none.

near.why: Fixation is the step that lets nitrogen gas enter living things, so the whole nitrogen cycle depends on it.
Legumes feed sugar to the bacteria in their nodules and get ammonia back, a mutualism you can dig up.
Only certain bacteria can break the strong bond in nitrogen gas; no plant or animal can.

phloem-transport.name: How sugar moves in a plant (phloem)
phloem-transport.blurb: Sugar made in leaves is pushed through living tubes toward the parts of the plant that use it.
phloem-transport.subject: biology
aliases: how does sugar move in a plant

rungs.adds: Morning glory vines: longer paths need source pressure from 0.75 to over 2.2 MPa.

near.why: The sugar moved here is what the plant made from sunlight, so phloem decides where that production ends up.
Water flowing into the sugar-loaded tubes by osmosis builds the pressure that pushes the sap along.
The sugar carried is mostly sucrose, and plants store the surplus as starch in roots, tubers and seeds.

photoperiodism.name: Day length and flowering (photoperiodism)
photoperiodism.blurb: Plants use a light-switching pigment and the length of the night to tell the season and time flowering.
photoperiodism.subject: biology
aliases: how do plants know when to flower

rungs.adds: Hamner and Bonner's cocklebur: vary light and dark separately; night length decides.

near.why: Plants must keep an internal clock to measure night length, as animals do for their daily rhythms.
Day length is the reliable cue that tells plants, and many animals, which season is coming.
Our eyes also carry a light sensor that reports day length to the brain's clock.

plant-hormones.name: Plant hormones
plant-hormones.blurb: Plants use chemicals made in small amounts to steer growth, ripening, dormancy and defence.
plant-hormones.subject: biology
aliases: what does ethylene do to fruit

rungs.adds: Auxin, ethylene and others, each with one effect; abscisic acid holds seeds dormant.

near.why: A hormone is a signal that binds a receptor and changes what a cell does, in plants as in animals.
Some plant hormones work by switching on genes through receptors, as steroid hormones do in animals.
Hormones such as gibberellin and abscisic acid decide when a resting seed wakes up.

plant-life-cycle.name: Plant life cycle
plant-life-cycle.blurb: A plant grows from a seed, flowers, makes new seeds, and dies, and the new seeds start the circle again.
plant-life-cycle.subject: biology
aliases: where do new beans come from
how does a seed become a plant

rungs.adds: Grow a bean plant from seed to seed over about three months.

near.why: A mealworm also passes through set stages, so you can compare how two living things grow up.
The cycle restarts when a seed wakes up; this lesson shows what a seed needs to do it.
The flower stage only leads to seeds if pollen reaches the right place, so go see how that happens.

plant-mineral-nutrition.name: Mineral nutrients for plants
plant-mineral-nutrition.blurb: Besides carbon dioxide and water, a plant needs mineral elements from the soil, and a shortage shows in its leaves.
plant-mineral-nutrition.subject: biology
aliases: how do plant roots take up minerals

rungs.adds: Leave one element out of Hoagland's solution, then read old versus young leaves.

near.why: The minerals a plant takes up come from soil, and soil's makeup decides how much is on offer.
Nitrogen is the mineral plants need most, and this cycle shows how it gets into the soil.
Most plant roots partner with fungi that reach farther into the soil and bring back minerals.
Root cells pull minerals in with pumps, even when the soil holds less than the cell does.

plant-parts.name: Parts of a plant and their jobs
plant-parts.blurb: Roots, stems, leaves, flowers and fruits each do a job that keeps a plant alive and making seeds.
plant-parts.subject: biology
aliases: what do roots stems and leaves do
is a tomato a fruit or a vegetable
which part of a plant is a carrot

rungs.adds: Sort groceries onto a drawn plant: carrot is a root, potato a stem.

near.why: Each plant part is made of cells, and each cell has its own parts doing small jobs.
Roots, stem and leaves are joined by tubes; this lesson shows how water travels through them.
Fruits and seeds are plant parts built to travel, so see how they get away from the parent.

plant-tropisms.name: How plants bend (tropisms)
plant-tropisms.blurb: A shoot or root bends toward or away from light or gravity because one side grows faster than the other.
plant-tropisms.subject: biology
aliases: why do plants grow toward light

rungs.adds: Split tips: same total auxin in light and dark, more from the shaded half.

near.why: A hormone that is more concentrated on one side tells cells there to grow differently, as in an embryo.
A plant has to turn light or gravity into a chemical signal, as eyes and ears do.
Plant cells sense gravity through heavy starch grains that settle onto their inner filament frame.

plant-water-transport.name: How water moves through a plant
plant-water-transport.blurb: Water is pulled up thin tubes from roots to leaves as it evaporates from the leaves.
plant-water-transport.subject: biology
aliases: how does water get to the top of a tree
why does celery soak up colored water

rungs.adds: Stand celery in blue water and watch the colour climb to the leaves.
Evaporating leaves pull the column up a tree; cohesion keeps it from breaking.
A redwood lifts water 100 metres with no pump: cohesion and tension.

near.why: How water gets into a root cell in the first place.
Leaves lose water through the pores that take in carbon dioxide.

plants-on-land.name: How plants live on land
plants-on-land.blurb: Plants moved onto land by evolving waxy coats, leaf pores, water tubes, pollen and seeds that cope with dry air.
plants-on-land.subject: biology

rungs.adds: Each innovation matched to its problem: drying, support, dry fertilization, dispersal.

near.why: Fossils show the first plants on land, and which features appeared before others.
The leaf pore is the land plant's main solution to dry air, and it brings its own trade-off.
Plants could only exist because an ancient cell took in a bacterium that became the chloroplast.
Fossil roots show fungi were partners of the first land plants, helping them find water and minerals.

pollination.name: Pollination
pollination.blurb: Pollen must travel to the sticky tip of a flower, carried by wind or animals, before the flower can make seeds.
pollination.subject: biology
aliases: how do bees help flowers make seeds

rungs.adds: Take a flower apart ring by ring, then play bee with coloured sugar pollen.
Darwin predicted a moth for a 30 cm orchid spur; wind versus animals.

near.why: Flower shape and pollinator body shape have changed together, as with a long flower and a long tongue.
Pollen carries genes from one plant to another, sometimes across long distances.
When pollinators decline, the plants that depend on them fall too, which affects many species.
Once pollen lands, the sperm still has to reach the egg; fertilization is that next step.

secondary-growth.name: How a trunk gets wider (wood and bark)
secondary-growth.blurb: A thin layer of dividing cells under the bark adds wood inward and bark outward, so stems thicken.
secondary-growth.subject: biology
aliases: how does a tree trunk get wider

rungs.adds: Same 2 mm ring, ten times the radius: 9.6 times the wood added.

near.why: Wood locks carbon away for centuries, so growing trunks hold part of the carbon taken from the air.
The cambium is a ring of dividing cells that keeps making new tissue on both sides.
Wood is old water-carrying tubes, so a trunk's wood is what lifts water to the top.

seed-dispersal.name: Seed dispersal
seed-dispersal.blurb: Plants cannot walk, so their seeds travel away from the parent by wind, water and animals.
seed-dispersal.subject: biology
aliases: how do plants spread their seeds
why do burrs stick to socks

rungs.adds: A sock walk catches hitchhiking seeds; then sort them and time maple keys.

near.why: A seed's wing, hook or fleshy fruit is an adaptation that gets it to new ground.
Seeds that land under the parent compete with it for light, water and soil, which is why travel helps.

A seed that travels well can also carry a plant to places where it crowds out others.

seed-germination.name: Seeds waking up (germination)
seed-germination.blurb: A dry seed is alive but resting; water and warmth wake it, and the root comes out first.
seed-germination.subject: biology
aliases: why seeds need water to sprout

Water switches on enzymes in the seed that break down its stored food for the first growth.
Once the root comes out it bends downward and the shoot bends upward, steered by gravity and light.

seeds-and-fruits.name: How seeds and fruits form
seeds-and-fruits.blurb: After fertilization the ovule becomes a seed and the ovary becomes a fruit, which can wait and travel.
seeds-and-fruits.subject: biology
aliases: how does a flower become a fruit
what part of the flower becomes the fruit
why is a strawberry not a true fruit
where does a seed come from in a flower

near.why: A fruit's form usually has a job in travel, such as floating, sticking to fur or being eaten.
The seed's food store is spent when it wakes, so see what happens when a dry seed gets water.
Crops such as wheat, corn and tomatoes were bred for bigger seeds and fruits over thousands of years.

stomata-and-water-loss.name: Stomata and water loss in leaves
stomata-and-water-loss.blurb: A leaf takes in carbon dioxide through tiny pores that also let water vapour out, so every gain of carbon costs water.
stomata-and-water-loss.subject: biology
aliases: why do plants close their pores

rungs.adds: Hundreds of water molecules lost per carbon dioxide gained; barley with fewer pores.

near.why: Water lost through the pores is what pulls more water up from the roots.

More carbon dioxide in the air lets plants keep their pores more closed, which changes their water use.
The pores admit the carbon dioxide that photosynthesis needs, so closing them slows sugar making.

acid-base-balance.name: Acid-base balance (blood pH)
acid-base-balance.blurb: Blood stays near pH 7.4 because buffers, the lungs and the kidneys keep bicarbonate and carbon dioxide in a steady ratio.
acid-base-balance.subject: biology

rungs.adds: Bicarbonate to dissolved CO2 near 20 to 1 sets pH; lungs fast, kidney slow.

near.why: Buffers are the first defence that keeps blood pH steady, before the lungs and kidneys adjust it.
Most carbon dioxide travels in blood as bicarbonate, the same partner that holds blood pH steady.
Breathing faster or slower changes how much carbon dioxide stays in blood, which moves its pH within minutes.

adrenal-glands.name: The adrenal glands
adrenal-glands.blurb: Small glands on top of the kidneys make salt, fuel and stress hormones in separate layers, each under its own control.
adrenal-glands.subject: biology
aliases: what do the adrenal glands do

rungs.adds: Zones decide what is made; 11-beta-HSD2 keeps cortisol off the aldosterone receptor.

near.why: Cortisol is made when a pituitary hormone calls for it, and cortisol then feeds back to turn that call down.
Cortisol and adrenaline raise blood sugar when the body is under stress, pushing against what insulin does.
The adrenal salt hormone aldosterone makes the kidney keep sodium and give up potassium.

baroreflex.name: The baroreflex
baroreflex.blurb: Stretch sensors in the big neck and chest arteries sense blood pressure, and the brainstem changes heart rate and vessels within seconds.
baroreflex.subject: biology
aliases: how the body corrects a change in blood pressure within seconds

rungs.adds: Gain of 2 removes two thirds of a fast pressure change.

near.why: The brainstem changes heart rate and vessel width through sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves, with no conscious choice.
The reflex corrects blood pressure in seconds, while the kidney decides the level it settles at over days.
A change in heart rate from the reflex changes how much blood the heart sends out each minute.

blood-clotting.name: Blood clotting (hemostasis)
blood-clotting.blurb: A cut vessel is sealed by a plug of platelets and a net of protein threads, while brakes keep clots from spreading.
blood-clotting.subject: biology

rungs.adds: Plasma, cells and the steps that seal a leak, compared with horseshoe crab.
A thrombin trickle on tissue cells, then a burst on platelets.

near.why: Clotting proteins are made switched off and are turned on one after another, only at the cut.
The clotting enzyme thrombin speeds up its own making, so a small cut triggers a fast, strong seal.
Platelets stick to collagen, a matrix protein, that is exposed when a vessel wall is cut.

blood-flow-resistance.name: Blood flow and resistance in vessels
blood-flow-resistance.blurb: Blood flows from high pressure to low, and the narrow small arteries hold most of the resistance and steer each organ's share.
blood-flow-resistance.subject: biology
aliases: where does blood pressure drop in the circulation
resistances in series and in parallel

rungs.adds: Resistance climbs with the fourth power of narrowing: arterioles steer flow, capillaries run slow.
Only about 15 percent of pressure falls across capillaries in cat muscle.

near.why: Pressure left after the small arteries decides how much fluid is pushed out through the thin capillary walls.
Working tissues widen their own small arteries, which lowers resistance and raises their share of the blood.
Total flow through all the vessels equals what the heart pumps, so resistance and heart output must agree.

blood-sugar.name: Blood sugar control
blood-sugar.blurb: Insulin and glucagon keep the sugar in your blood steady between meals and after them.
blood-sugar.subject: biology
aliases: why does blood sugar stay steady after a meal
how does the body store sugar

rungs.adds: Glucose as a loop: beta cells, insulin, and glucagon between meals.
One insulin-to-glucagon ratio, read differently by liver, muscle and fat.

near.why: Blood sugar is held steady by negative feedback.
Once glucose is inside a cell, this is how the energy comes out.

body-temperature.name: Keeping warm and keeping cool
body-temperature.blurb: Animals stay at a working temperature by balancing the heat they make and gain against the heat they lose.
body-temperature.subject: biology

rungs.adds: Dip a shortening-lined mitten in ice water and feel fat hold heat in.
Heat made plus heat gained equals heat lost: lizards, mammals, fever, hibernation.
Sweat cools only if it evaporates, and humid air sets a ceiling.

near.why: Temperature control is one feedback loop among many.
Blubber, fur and feathers are adaptations for the same job.
Skin senses warm and cold, which is how the loop gets its news.

body-water-compartments.name: Body water and its compartments
body-water-compartments.blurb: Body water sits in two places, inside cells and outside them, and the outside part splits into tissue fluid and plasma.
body-water-compartments.subject: biology
aliases: how much of the body is water
where is the water in your body

rungs.adds: Reference man: 42 L of water, 28 inside cells, measured by dilution.

near.why: Water crosses cell membranes toward more dissolved stuff, which sets how body water divides between cells and the rest.
When fluid collects in the space between cells faster than it is drained, the tissue swells.
Animals keep these compartments steady by matching every gain and loss of water and salt.

bone-remodeling.name: Bone remodeling
bone-remodeling.blurb: Bone is rebuilt all your life: some cells dissolve old patches while others lay down new bone in their place.
bone-remodeling.subject: biology

rungs.adds: Remodeling is set by RANKL against OPG: excess OPG in mice gave dense bone.

near.why: Bone holds most of the body's calcium, and dissolving or building it is how blood calcium is kept steady.
Bone is mostly matrix that cells make around themselves, then harden with mineral.

breathing.name: Breathing and its control
breathing.blurb: Muscles enlarge the chest to pull air into the lungs, and the carbon dioxide in your blood sets how hard you breathe.
breathing.subject: biology
aliases: how do lungs fill with air

rungs.adds: Mammals pull air in, frogs pump it; carbon dioxide, not oxygen, sets resting breathing.
Follow pleural pressure from -5 to -8 cmH2O; compliance is 0.17 L per cmH2O.

near.why: A soapy lung coating lets tiny air sacs open, so the chest does not have to pull so hard to fill them.
Once air is in the lungs, oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the thin wall by diffusion.
The diaphragm and rib muscles enlarge the chest by shortening, which is sliding filaments at work.

calcium-balance.name: Calcium and phosphate balance
calcium-balance.blurb: The body keeps the free calcium in blood in a narrow range using parathyroid hormone, vitamin D, the gut, kidneys and bone.
calcium-balance.subject: biology
aliases: how the body controls blood calcium

rungs.adds: Calcium sensor sets PTH; PTH opens kidney, bone and gut doors, throws phosphate out.

near.why: Bone is the calcium store, so each swing in blood calcium is met by dissolving or laying down bone.
Cells keep calcium very low inside, so a small rise works as a message, and blood calcium must stay steady.
Calcium is the switch that lets muscle pull, so too little or too much in blood upsets muscle work.

capillary-exchange.name: Fluid exchange across capillaries (Starling forces)
capillary-exchange.blurb: Blood pressure pushes fluid out through capillary walls, plasma proteins pull some back, and lymph vessels return the rest.
capillary-exchange.subject: biology
aliases: what does the lymphatic system do

rungs.adds: Push out minus pull in: Landis timed trapped red cells in frog capillaries.
Starling's reabsorbing venous end fails: filtration all along, set by Pc, Pi, albumin.

near.why: When fluid leaves capillaries faster than lymph vessels remove it, the tissue swells.
Plasma proteins hold water in the blood by osmosis, which is the pull that balances the pressure pushing fluid out.
The pressure in the capillary comes from how much resistance the small arteries before it have used up.

carbon-dioxide-transport.name: How blood carries carbon dioxide
carbon-dioxide-transport.blurb: Blood carries carbon dioxide back to the lungs mostly as bicarbonate, with a little dissolved and a little on hemoglobin.
carbon-dioxide-transport.subject: biology
aliases: how is carbon dioxide carried in blood

rungs.adds: About 85% as bicarbonate, 10% dissolved, 5% on hemoglobin in resting tissue.

near.why: The bicarbonate that carries carbon dioxide is also the main buffer that holds blood pH steady.
Hemoglobin carries both gases in opposite directions, and carbon dioxide arriving helps it let go of oxygen.
Carbon dioxide leaves the blood and oxygen enters it by diffusion across the lung or gill surface.

cardiac-cycle.name: The cardiac cycle (pressure-volume loop)
cardiac-cycle.blurb: Each heartbeat fills, squeezes, ejects and relaxes in four steps, set by when the heart valves open and close.
cardiac-cycle.subject: biology

rungs.adds: Where two lines meet: stroke volume from Ea and Ees, and why EF misleads.

near.why: The electrical waves on a skin trace come just before each fill and squeeze step of the heartbeat.
Each beat's volume, multiplied by heart rate, gives the blood the heart sends out each minute.
Each squeeze of the heart is heart muscle shortening, using the same sliding filaments and calcium switch.

cardiac-output.name: Cardiac output and venous return
cardiac-output.blurb: The heart can pump out only the blood that returns to it, so output settles where the heart and veins balance.
cardiac-output.subject: biology
aliases: how much blood does the heart pump each minute

rungs.adds: Output is where two curves cross: stressed volume, Guyton's dogs, and the Fick calculation.

near.why: Output is set partly by how much resistance the small arteries put in the way of the blood.
Pressure sensors in the arteries change heart rate within seconds, which changes output.
The oxygen a body can use each minute depends on how much blood the heart can send out.

circadian-rhythm.name: Daily body clocks (circadian rhythm)
circadian-rhythm.blurb: Living things have an inner clock that repeats about every 24 hours and is kept in step by light and dark.
circadian-rhythm.subject: biology
aliases: why do I get sleepy at night
how do plants know what time it is

neuronal-migration.name: Neuron migration

pattern-completion.name: Pattern completion in networks

reward-prediction-error.name: Reward prediction error (dopamine and learning)

reward-prediction-error.subject: biology

semaphorins.name: Semaphorins (repulsive cues)

sleep-regulation.name: What decides when we sleep

split-brain.name: The split brain

spontaneous-activity.name: Spontaneous activity (retinal waves)

spontaneous-activity.subject: biology

tumour-suppressor.name: Tumour suppressors

two-component-system.name: Two-component systems in bacteria

wnt-signaling.name: Wnt signaling (β-catenin)

cell-fate.name: How embryo cells get their fates

cortical-expansion.name: Why the human cortex is big

early-embryo.name: How an embryo begins (cleavage and gastrulation)

fertilization.name: Fertilization

how does an egg block extra sperm

hox-genes.name: Hox genes
hox-genes.blurb: A family of genes whose order on the chromosome matches the order of body regions they label from head to tail.

interkinetic-nuclear-migration.name: Interkinetic nuclear migration

interkinetic-nuclear-migration.subject: biology

nucleus moves with the cell cycle

lateral-inhibition.name: Lateral inhibition between equal neighbours

lateral-inhibition.subject: biology

how two identical cells take opposite fates
how does only one cell in a cluster become a neuron
